verdict.rationale: Both reviews find the two blockers (SQL injection in search, swallowed audit errors), back them with reproductions, and give accurate line references. B also flags that the audit `actor` comes straight from the request parameters, which matters for the compliance audit trail the PR exists to deliver; A misses this. B also catches more verified edge cases: duplicate ids producing two audit rows, and negative `per_page` returning every user. A's review is accurate and well prioritised, but B's is more complete on the issues that matter.
a_issues: Misses that the audit `actor` is taken from client-supplied request params, so the audit trail can be forged
Misses duplicate ids producing duplicate audit rows, and negative per_page acting as no limit
audit.py line range 14-16 is slightly off (the except/pass is at 15-16)
b_issues: Somewhat longer, and the merge condition (#1-#6 all before merge) is stricter than needed
The claim that the injection can read other tables is asserted without a demonstration
